title: First brass band job with the Excelsior and marching technique
summary: Alcorn recalls his first brass band job, sent to sub with the Excelsior Brass Band around 1929-30, the lineup that day, the band's instrumentation, and how bass drum and left-foot marching work for 6/8 and 2/4 marches.

story.theme_name: Brass bands, parades and jazz funerals
story.community_name: Parading for Mardi Gras and the clubs

blocks.x: I was a member of a group of brass bands. So you become a member then? You don't get elected a member. No, it's just a guy who used to join his band and you join him. And when you cut out you just tell him, well I think I'm going with so and so. It's not a contract, it's just a word. That's all it is. What was the first brass band you ever worked? I think the Excelsior Brass Band was the first brass band I worked. It was in Jordan McCullum's place he sent me. He was a regular member of the brass band. And if I'm not mistaken he couldn't get off one day from his work so he sent me over to work with the band. And that particular day was Mania Perez, Peter, Peter Bogart, myself that was the trumpets. It was Buddy Johnson, Tremont. Harrison Barnes, Tremont. Henry Martin, bass drum. That's real mama who was on snare now. That's real mama. His brother, Henry Boca Eyes, Pete's brother Henry was playing bass. A fellow his name was Joe Payane, he played French malaphone. And I'm trying to think who was playing clarinet that day. My brother was out of town too I think if I'm not mistaken. How do you spell Payane? I never could, or do you not? No I don't, because I never get the right pronunciation of the name. You know everybody used to say it different ways. But he was like a little manager of the band. He used to get all awake, you know, for the Excelsior Brass Band. He was the leader and he was the manager. Did they have a set up with the saxophones at all then, or did they have a baritone on or what? No they used to use a saxophone. That was the reed instrument. At one time I understand they used to use clarinet. But when Oliver went with the band he wasn't playing clarinet, you know, for brass band music. So they put him on alto, he played alto saxophone. Did they have him and Joe Payane at the same time? Yeah, he played sort of French horn, I mean peck-on, you know. Yeah, well now what kind of part would they carry? It was alto saxophone. They had an alto saxophone part and an alto horn. That's right. I see. They didn't have a baritone horn then, huh, or did they? Yeah, they was using the baritone. The baritone horn was Vic Gasper. And sometimes Vic used to play a trumon but he mostly used to play baritone with the band, Vic Gasper. That about fills the band out. Did you ever work with any of the Matthews brothers with drummers, other than Bill? I know you played. I worked with his brother Remus too. I didn't work with others. Bebe. Bebe and Emno, I didn't know very much of Bebe. But I did work with a, at this time, the time I speak, my Bill was playing with my brother named George McCollum's band. He was playing trumon with George McCollum's band at the time. What year was it you think that you first started playing the street? I think it was about 29 or 30, something like that. So it was when you were just getting started? Yeah, but I hadn't been playing very long. Well that was a real honor to be sent with the Excelsior. Well it was a fine band. But I mean if you were that young and just started, I bet you were trembling. No I wasn't. No? No, because in those days I mean they mostly played music. And we used to stay in the Method all the time so if anything you play in the Method you still could play in the street you see. So they were just playing funeral marches and I was well schooled with six eighths and all like that from coming out of an Auburn Method. So I mean it was just actually walking in the street and playing with a group instead of playing with just two of us. Like with George and I used to run through all types of marches together. There's duets and things you know, two trumpets. Did you have any trouble with the marching? No. Just you just started? I just looked at them before they'd play them and then play them on the album. No I mean did you get confused about which foot you were going on? No, no. I was always schooled on that too. Oh, who would teach you that? The left foot? George? The teacher, yeah. He showed you how to walk off and everything. So you've got to be careful when you do that. Oh yeah. Especially if you're playing something you've never read before. But after you know it too and you just walk any type of way you want with it, you see, and that depends on the time. But when you're first starting off you're so tickling. Well that walking helps you keep the time of the music. Yeah well you know it, that's right, you see. Every first beat is your left foot, you see. Well then you, how did the bass drums start off a march or a dirge those times? Would they just go boom, boom, boom? No. Or would they go boom, boom, boom, boom. That's four beats you see. The last two beats is right behind each other, like boom, boom. And then what foot would you hit right after that boom, boom? Boom, boom, boom, boom, boom. Then you'd step out with your left foot right there and see. I see. And you start off. Then you're ready for the first beat in the next measure. Starting the tune. Boom. You're right there with that. So you know exactly how to step out. That's right. And the first beat of every measure is going to be on your left foot then. On the left. So I hadn't even thought about 6-8. 6-8 the same way. Yeah I guess it would come out, yeah. See, because you knock it off the same way. Boom, boom, boom, boom, boom, boom, boom, boom, boom, boom, boom, boom, boom, boom, boom, boom, boom, boom, boom. The bass drum give you the same way. Yeah they played 2-4 and 4-4. There's not many 6-8s anymore. You don't play a few more. No, you don't get very many 6-8s much. I don't know. Does John play 6-8s? Yeah I tell you when they used to use quite a few 6-8s, we don't play very many of them now. But like we used to play for a drilling group like the Patriarchs or the Odd Fellows or something like that, used to have that drilling group. Well they like playing more. So we used to play quite a few 6-8s for them. But ordinary playing that lib music, most of the guys play for like clubs, they mostly like wild lib music, like blueses and different things like that, you know. That blues beat, something like that. Not that stiff, you know, just 6-8s.
